restated: Does the CPython Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) prevent all parallelism, or does it only restrict parallel execution of Python bytecode?

sub_questions.question: What is the CPython Global Interpreter Lock and how does it affect the execution of Python bytecode in multiple threads?
sub_questions.search_query: CPython GIL execution of Python bytecode threads
sub_questions.why: Provides the definition of the GIL and explains that it serializes bytecode execution across threads, establishing the baseline for parallelism restrictions.

sub_questions.question: Under what circumstances does the CPython GIL get released, allowing other threads to run concurrently?
sub_questions.search_query: CPython GIL released during I/O blocking calls
sub_questions.why: Shows that the GIL is not permanently held; it is released during blocking I/O or long-running C operations, enabling some concurrent activity.

sub_questions.question: How do C extensions and the multiprocessing module interact with the CPython GIL to enable parallel execution?
sub_questions.search_query: C extensions release GIL multiprocessing CPython
sub_questions.why: Explains that C extensions can explicitly release the GIL and that multiprocessing spawns separate interpreter instances, both providing true parallelism beyond bytecode execution.

sub_questions.question: Does the CPython GIL prevent all forms of parallelism, or only the parallel execution of Python bytecode?
sub_questions.why: Summarizes the overall impact, confirming that the GIL restricts only Python bytecode execution in threads, while other mechanisms still allow parallelism.

assumptions: The question refers to the CPython implementation of Python.
Parallelism is considered in the context of CPU-bound and I/O-bound operations.
The user is interested in both thread-based and process-based concurrency.
